claims.text: Pre-exposure Q235 steel has a native oxide on its surface.
Optimized plasma nitriding of Q235 steel produces a uniform nitrogen-enriched surface nitride layer.
The nitrided layer has altered electronic structure relative to the native oxide film.
The nitrogen-enriched nitride layer stabilizes the passive film.
The nitride layer acts as a barrier against chloride ingress.
Reduced chloride ingress limits active metal dissolution.
A nonuniform or inadequately formed nitride layer compromises the proposed protective mechanism.
Optimally nitrided Q235 steel will exhibit delayed corrosion initiation relative to untreated Q235 steel in chloride-rich environments.
Optimally nitrided Q235 steel will exhibit reduced pit density relative to untreated Q235 steel.
Optimally nitrided Q235 steel will exhibit lower overall corrosion rates relative to untreated Q235 steel.
The proposed corrosion protection will operate at both room temperature and 80°C.
The protective effect requires a uniform, defect-free nitride layer.
Deviations in nitride-layer thickness or formation may limit corrosion suppression.
The achievable uniformity of a plasma-nitrided layer on Q235 steel is uncertain.
The long-term stability of the nitrided layer under cyclic temperature conditions is uncertain.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis states that plasma nitriding produces a uniform layer and the intervention proposes ensuring one, while the uncertainty field says that achieving such uniformity on Q235 steel remains uncertain.

The mechanism and boundary fields state that a nonuniform layer means the protective mechanism was not successfully instantiated, but the falsification rule treats a nonuniform layer correlated with poor corrosion performance as falsification of the mechanism. That result would instead indicate treatment or mediator failure unless protection had also been tested with a confirmed uniform layer.
